An oracle that selects with realized labels is an \emph{ex-post} benchmark. Part of its advantage is unreachable by construction: when outcomes are random given the covariates, some feasible label set will turn out to be lucky, and only hindsight can find it. The distinction between ex-post and ex-ante regret is familiar in decision-focused learning and robust optimization~\cite{schutte2023robust}, and in bandits the gap between expected regret and pseudo-regret grows with the noise of the arms~\cite{bubeck2012regret,audibert2010regret}. It has not been measured for oracle bounds in label acquisition, where it decides whether an ``oracle gap'' signals room for better strategies or merely outcome noise. Labels in credit, healthcare and marketing record stochastic outcomes rather than near-deterministic categories, so the question matters most where labels are bought with consequential actions.

\paragraph{Benchmark oracle.} Benchmarks use a greedy oracle that adds the feasible candidate whose realized label most reduces loss on the evaluation set, and score it on the same set~\cite{werner2023comparable,werner2024cdalbench}. We split the test labels into halves $T_1,T_2$ and report three quantities over replicates $Y^{(r)}$ of the training labels: the \emph{reported} gap (oracle selects and is scored on $T_1$), the \emph{ex-post} gap (same oracle scored on $T_2$), and the \emph{deployable} gap of an ex-ante greedy oracle that selects by mean $T_1$ loss over half the replicates and is scored on $T_2$ over the other half. Then
\[
\text{reported}=\underbrace{(\text{reported}-\text{ex-post})}_{\text{test reuse}}+\underbrace{(\text{ex-post}-\text{deployable})}_{\text{aleatoric floor}}+\text{deployable}.
\]
The ex-ante oracle is itself greedy, so the deployable gap may be underestimated and the reuse-plus-floor share overestimated; we therefore read that share as an upper bound.

\paragraph{Estimation without known probabilities.} Given outcome probabilities $p$, we draw $R$ replicates of the hidden training labels and evaluate every set on all replicates with common random numbers. The plug-in $\widehat H_{\mathrm{pre}}$ is biased upward by selecting on noise~\cite{smith2006optimizer,cawley2010overfitting} and a two-fold cross-fitted estimate~\cite{chernozhukov2018double} downward, so they bracket $H_{\mathrm{pre}}$. On real data $p$ is unknown; we replace it by $\hat p$ from gradient boosting fitted on cohort records disjoint from the state (up to 20{,}000), and score test loss on the recorded test labels. The recorded training outcomes give one draw of every set's loss, so the realized hindsight gap $\bar L(M;y)-\min_S\bar L(S;y)$ is model-free and its mean must match the $\hat p$-based $H_{\mathrm{post}}$.

\paragraph{Estimated probabilities recover known-probability values.} On 512 semi-synthetic states, boosting $\hat p$ fitted on auxiliary records labeled from the true $p$ gives estimates whose bias against the known-$p$ protocol lies within $\pm0.5$ in 95 of 96 checks (8 groups $\times$ 12 quantities); mean biases of $H_{\mathrm{post}}$, $H_{\mathrm{pre}}$, the floor and the main strategy gains are at most $0.20$, with state-level correlations of $0.73$--$0.95$ for $H_{\mathrm{pre}}$. A logistic $\hat p$ underestimates $H_{\mathrm{pre}}$ by $0.26$--$0.28$ where the truth is nonlinear, so the estimator needs a flexible $\hat p$.

\paragraph{The estimator is calibrated on recorded outcomes.} With the logistic and boosting learners, the $\hat p$-based $H_{\mathrm{post}}$ agrees with the mean model-free realized gap in all 16 cohort--learner cells of the eight cohorts and in all 8 credit cells of an independent 128-seed batch (every 95\% interval contains zero). With the neural learner it agrees in 8 of 9 cohorts; on PPDai it overstates the realized gap ($7.4$ against $5.0$, difference $2.4$ $[0.6,4.2]$), a limit of the substitution that we flag in the results.

\paragraph{The decomposition does not depend on the family.} Enlarging each family with 64 random feasible sets (from 22--27 to 81--88 sets) leaves the deployable share $H_{\mathrm{pre}}/H_{\mathrm{post}}$ essentially unchanged: 80--83\% in controlled worlds at every sub-family size from 2 to 80, and 6--38\% on semi-synthetic arms, where it rises slightly rather than falls with $|\mathcal F|$.

\paragraph{The floor's share rises with label noise.} Before running the eight-cohort study we registered that the floor's share of the oracle gap would be smaller on the two cohorts with the lowest noise index (mean $\hat p(1-\hat p)$ over candidates) and would increase with that index. Both held (Table~\ref{tab:gradient}): the lowest-noise cohorts, Spambase and USPS, had a floor share of 14\% against 59\% for the other six, and the Spearman correlation between noise index and floor share was $0.83$ (logistic learner) and $0.67$ (neural learner). On USPS with raw pixels and a neural learner, the setting of a recent benchmark~\cite{werner2024cdalbench}, the floor is 10\% of the oracle gap and the oracle's lead remains $8.0$ after correction: the benchmark's message that strategies leave room is largely sound there. On credit, readmission and marketing outcomes, 58--100\% (logistic) and 67--93\% (neural) of the lead is reuse and floor. Test reuse is a separate, noise-independent bias: it is up to a third of the reported gap on Spambase and larger with the neural learner.

\paragraph{The floor is predictable.} Across all studies, the measured family floor lies between the two-leader lower bound~\eqref{eq:two} and the independent-normal upper bound in all 87 cohort--learner--budget settings (Fig.~\ref{fig:floor}a). The lower bound is tight up to a near-constant factor: the measured floor is about 2.7 times~\eqref{eq:two} with $R^2=0.92$ (logistic) and $0.97$ (boosting) across groups, and state-level Spearman correlations of $0.68$ and $0.85$. The floor depends on the learner, as the bracket predicts through $s$: with the same states and labels it spans $0.7$--$4.4$ for the logistic learner and $0.9$--$8.3$ for boosting, and the benchmark-oracle floor is $0.8$--$2.3$ for the logistic and $1.8$--$4.9$ for the neural learner. Whereas the deployable gap varies by two orders of magnitude across settings, the floor stays within one, so hindsight comparisons mislead most where true differences are small. Fig.~\ref{fig:floor}b shows the registered noise ordering for both learners.

\paragraph{A risk budget raises the floor.} The bracket implies that admitting more random outcomes raises the floor. We registered that the floor would increase with the risk budget and varied $k$ in $B_t$ from 3 to 6 to 12 (Fig.~\ref{fig:budget}). The floor rose monotonically in all eight cohorts, from $0.32$--$0.87$ at $k=3$ to $0.91$--$1.90$ at $k=12$ (pooled paired increase $0.74$ $[0.67,0.82]$), and the bracket held at every budget. The mean outcome variance of the reference set changed by at most $0.02$ within a cohort, so the increase comes from acquiring more random outcomes rather than riskier ones. In risk-constrained acquisition the budget therefore controls how far an oracle comparison can be trusted.

\paragraph{Who closes the deployable gap depends on the learner.} Table~\ref{tab:who} reports, on the same real-label states, the deployable gap and the gains of three strategies under two learners. With the logistic learner, information proxies derived from that model close a large part of it where it is largest: on engineered HMEQ and LendingClub TargetVar-greedy and Proxy-argmax capture $1.5$--$2.1$ of $3.2$--$3.4$ (in an independent 128-seed batch, $2.5$--$2.9$ of $4.9$--$5.7$, while DC-PRISM trails TargetVar-greedy by $2.8$ $[0.0,5.6]$ on LendingClub). With the boosting learner the deployable gap is still $0.7$--$2.7$, DC-PRISM's selection gap is material in six of eight credit cells, and no strategy captures more than $0.65$: proxies that match the logistic model do not transfer to the boosting learner. On readmission the deployable gap is small ($0.7$--$0.9$) and no strategy differs decisively.

\paragraph{DC-PRISM in controlled worlds.} In worlds built around directional pending information, 83\% of hindsight headroom is deployable and DC-PRISM captures two thirds of it: its gain over Safe-MinRisk is $12.2$ $[7.6,16.8]$ with $3.1$ instead of 6 labels, and remains material in all twelve generator variants we tried ($10.8$--$31.4$; pending overlap, risk--information coupling, no misspecified tail, 48 candidates with $K=12$). A common-family ablation attributes this gain to the proxy evaluated over an anchored family (Proxy-argmax alone gains $13.1$ $[6.1,20.2]$); the conservative layer adds an unconfirmed $3.0$ $[-0.2,6.2]$, and pending-awareness is not isolated by our evidence.

\paragraph{Regret notions and uncertainty.} Ex-ante and ex-post regret are distinguished in decision-focused learning and robust optimization~\cite{schutte2023robust}; expected regret exceeds pseudo-regret by a noise term in bandits~\cite{bubeck2012regret,audibert2010regret}; proper scoring rules such as the Brier score separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty~\cite{hofman2024quantifying}; and selecting the best of noisy estimates is optimistic~\cite{smith2006optimizer,cawley2010overfitting}, the value of perfect information being classical~\cite{howard1966information,raiffa1961applied}. We bring these ideas to oracle bounds for label acquisition and make the aleatoric part measurable and predictable on real data.

\paragraph{Acquisition under risk and delay.} Acquisition criteria range from uncertainty and transductive design to Fisher information, mutual and predictive information and decision loss~\cite{cohn1996active,settles2009active,lewis1994sequential,yu2006transductive,ash2021fishing,kirsch2019batchbald,bickfordsmith2023prediction,huang2026loss,chaloner1995bayesian}; budgets and knapsack constraints are handled by greedy selection~\cite{krause2005near,sviridenko2004note,tomanek2010cost}. Selective labels~\cite{lakkaraju2017selective,wei2021selective,kilbertus2020fair,keswani2024partial,crook2004reject}, safe exploration and safe active learning~\cite{sui2015safe,schreiter2015safe,wu2016conservative} and delayed feedback~\cite{joulani2013delayed,chapelle2014delayed,pham2022latency} motivate the risk-constrained setting in which we study the floor.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Learners and pools are small (logistic, small boosting and one-hidden-layer networks; 24 candidates, 6--256 features); large pretrained models were not studied. The deployable gap is measured with a greedy ex-ante oracle, so the reuse-plus-floor share is an upper bound. The real-data estimator needs a flexible $\hat p$ from disjoint records; it failed calibration once (PPDai, neural learner), and in lending those records contain only approved applicants~\cite{crook2004reject}. Multiclass benchmarks were binarized, splits are random rather than temporal, BAIT-greedy and TargetVar-greedy are adaptations, and the envelope's guarantee is not implied by our risk scores, although realized exceedance stayed far below $\alpha$. Code, frozen protocols with commit hashes, aggregate results and verifiers are available in an anonymized repository.
